item.title: The Part of You That's Always Somewhere Else
item.description:
Psychology

The Part of You That's Always Somewhere Else

This is the story behind the ego.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • The mind that seems present in conversation is often narrating instead of listening.
  • EMDR sessions can feel powerful, yet change nothing, if the narrator—not the self—does the work.
  • Noticing the narration in real-time—not understanding it—is what lets real change begin.

I just came back from a conference where I presented on how to prepare clients before they process traumatic memories with EMDR. One of the ideas I shared was that before asking the brain to revisit and reorganize painful experiences, we need to make sure the Self is the one in the room doing the work.

The suggestion raised an obvious question: Who else could be there?

Telling a therapist that they may be dealing with the ego can sound strangely non-clinical. We use the word "ego" so casually that it has almost become an insult because it carries the idea of arrogance, self-importance, defensiveness, or fakeness. That’s why I tried to name it something else.

The Narrator

Source: Image by Jean-Louis SERVAIS Pixabay

In my first book, I tried “hollow self” because I thought "ego" lacked substance. Once I understood its neurobiology better, I thought calling it “the narration self” was more appropriate because narrating is what this relational actor does.

Framing it as a "narrator" is useful because it allows us to understand its purpose within the system. Its main job is maintaining a coherent, defensible story about who you are. That story needs constant upkeep, so while you're living your actual life, some portion of your attention is somewhere else, reviewing what just happened, deciding what it meant, rehearsing how you'll describe it later, patching the version of events that keeps the story intact. As you may notice, its functioning still includes the self-referential “obsession” that gets most of the criticism, but it’s not a flaw. It’s a task.

Neurobiologically, the narrating self is what develops strongly when a brain network, specifically the default mode network, takes over the show, because the deeper circuits that would otherwise organize real connection never got the activation they needed. Often, it’s because the people we depended on early on weren't consistently there for us or for our needs. What it means is that the person's brain built the narrator as the best available solution: a way to make sense of needing someone who couldn't always be counted on.

An important characteristic is that it doesn’t operate in the present even when it’s consuming a lot of energy in real time. The self should be the one assimilating the story, but if it gets hijacked by the narrator, part of what’s actually happening gets lost.

The cost of this is bigger than it sounds. A mind spending most of its resources reviewing and patching a story has very little left over for attending reality. Curiosity requires spare attention, and the narrating self doesn't have any to spare.

article continues after advertisement

You can see this most clearly in a conversation. You are telling someone something that matters to you, and they're nodding, seemingly present, but clearly drafting their response, already telling you something comparable about them, equating it to something that happened last week. They're not actually curious about what you're saying. They're managing what it means for their story.

This is why I suggested paying attention to who's actually present during a session: Is it the narrator or the self doing the processing? And what kind of memory is being worked on? Is it a memory that's become part of the narrative? Or one that still carries its own emotional charge, separate from the story built around it?

I’ve experienced it with my clients and seen it happening to some of my supervisees. The client leaves an EMDR session after having done a lot of heavy lifting, with a lot of information showing up about the past, with deep emotional moments, and still reporting the same negative cognition, the same level of upset, and not really believing in the resolution they found. The narrating self can be really moved and generate lots of new material, giving the clinician the impression that another memory channel opened, while for the client, it feels more like another chapter, another piece of evidence for or against the version of themselves the narrator is maintaining.

One of the main messages of my talk was to notice that in those cases, the felt experience didn’t actually land anywhere, because the one doing the work was not looking to receive it.

This also means that explaining the concept of the narrating self to a client without an active intervention won’t change it. The narrating self will simply absorb the explanation and probably turn it into new material that helps it sound interested and interesting: another paragraph in the story, proof of how special they are if the story is about being unique, or how damaged they are if the narrative is about victimhood.

Still, this actor has real value, for the clinician and for the client. Knowing how the brain works, and how this type of issue runs automatically, draining our resources, can motivate change. Explaining that the narration has been working harder than it needs to, and that adjusting it will release some of that overload, could be life-changing.

article continues after advertisement

The idea that the ego should be controlled or eliminated is not new. It’s been said it's extensible in different contexts. But the approach I’m suggesting is about observing it as opposed to annihilating it. What can actually interrupt it is to work on developing another relational actor: the observing self.

It’s easier to build a new circuit than to change an already consolidated one.

The Observing Self

Source: Image by Gerd Altmann Pixabay

An observing self is a mode of activation that develops by noticing, in real-time, the narration, mid-sentence, the way you'd catch yourself starting to draft a reply while someone is still talking. That noticing has to be rehearsed. It doesn't develop on its own, and it doesn't develop quickly. First, it requires acknowledging that the narrator is an internal actor that has been running things. Then, it requires deliberate practice, the same way any underused capacity gets stronger through repetition, engagement, and intention. Having a therapist who knows to work toward that capacity specifically is of great help too.

I have to confess that my biases and previous understanding of the ego made me overlook its purpose. The self doesn't come back online because the narrating self finally ran out of things to say. It comes back online when there is a better understanding and connection with the narrator. You come to understand that the narrator exists because you were trying to make sense of people who could hurt you and still be the ones you depended on. But the narrator, like every other mechanism in us, has a positive intention and will stay quiet during processing if it gets that the system needs closure to heal—when the narrator becomes a supportive witness.

item.title: Is Excessive Guilt Holding You Back?
item.description:
Guilt

Is Excessive Guilt Holding You Back?

Guilt should be a guide, not an emotional burden.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Guilt can be adaptive or excessive, and it is important to know whether or not guilt is reasonable.
  • The Guilt Equation is a tool to identify the sources of guilt and to evaluate whether it is justified.
  • Four types of excessive guilt are perfectionism, people pleasing, over-responsibility, and control illusions.

Many of us carry guilt as though it were a badge of responsibility. We feel guilty for saying no, guilty for setting boundaries, guilty for taking time for ourselves, and sometimes even guilty for our successes. In her book Guilt Free: Reclaiming Your Life from Unreasonable Expectations, psychiatrist Jennifer Reid argues that much of the guilt we experience comes not from actual wrongdoing, but from unrealistic expectations and social conditioning. Reid offers practical tools, including her “Guilt Equation” and a framework for understanding the “Four Furies” that drive excessive guilt.

When Guilt Is Helpful

Not all guilt is bad. In psychology, guilt is considered an emotion that can serve an important adaptive function. Adaptive guilt occurs when we recognize that we have violated one of our values, hurt someone, or behaved in a way inconsistent with who we want to be.

For example, if you forget an important commitment to a friend and feel guilty, that emotion may motivate you to apologize, make amends, and strengthen the relationship. In this sense, guilt acts as an internal compass. It helps us maintain accountability, empathy, and connection with others.

Adaptive guilt is typically:

  • Linked to a specific behavior
  • Proportional to the situation
  • Temporary
  • Motivating rather than paralyzing
  • Resolved through repair, reparation, or corrective action

When Guilt Becomes Excessive

Excessive guilt is different. Rather than serving as a guide, it becomes an emotional burden. Excessive guilt often emerges when people assume responsibility for circumstances beyond their control or hold themselves to impossible standards.

A working mother may feel guilty for attending an important meeting rather than a school event. A caregiver may feel guilty for taking a needed afternoon off. A student may feel guilty for resting after weeks of hard work.

In these situations, no ethical violation has occurred. Yet, the emotional experience can be intense.

According to Reid, women are especially vulnerable to excessive guilt because they are often socialized to prioritize others' needs above their own and to equate self-sacrifice with virtue. As a result, guilt can become "sticky," lingering long after it has served any useful purpose.

Excessive guilt often sounds like:

  • "I should be doing more."
  • "I am letting someone down."
  • "A good person would be able to handle this better."
  • "If someone is unhappy, it must be my fault."

Unlike adaptive guilt, excessive guilt is tied less to actual behavior and more to unrealistic expectations.

The Guilt Equation (Guilt = Expectations - Reality)

One of Reid's key contributions is what she calls the Guilt Equation, a tool designed to help individuals identify the sources of their guilt and evaluate whether that guilt is justified. The equation encourages people to examine the expectations driving their emotional responses and to determine whether those expectations are realistic, fair, or even their own.

The central question becomes: Am I feeling guilty because I have violated one of my values or because I have failed to meet an unreasonable expectation?

This distinction is powerful. When guilt originates from a values violation, action may be needed. When guilt stems from an unrealistic standard, self-compassion and boundary-setting may be the healthier response.

The Four Furies of Guilt

Reid describes four common drivers that fuel excessive guilt, referred to as the "Four Furies of Unreasonable Expectations." These drivers often distort our perception of responsibility and keep us trapped in cycles of self-blame.

Although the specific manifestations vary from person to person, the Four Furies commonly involve:

  1. Perfectionism. The belief that mistakes are unacceptable and that we must perform flawlessly in all roles. Perfectionism creates a moving target that can never truly be achieved.
  2. People-Pleasing. The tendency to prioritize others' approval over our own needs. When saying yes becomes automatic, guilt frequently appears whenever we attempt to say no.
  3. Excessive Responsibility. The assumption that we are responsible for other people's feelings, outcomes, or well-being. This can leave individuals carrying burdens that were never theirs to carry.
  4. Illusions of Control. The belief that with enough effort, planning, or sacrifice, we can prevent disappointment, conflict, or suffering. When reality inevitably proves otherwise, guilt emerges.

These four drivers often work together, creating a nearly impossible standard: Be perfect, keep everyone happy, control every outcome, and never put yourself first.

A More Compassionate Way Forward

Freedom from excessive guilt does not mean becoming selfish or indifferent. Rather, it means learning to distinguish between responsibility and over-responsibility.

Adaptive guilt can help us grow. Excessive guilt keeps us stuck.

When we pause to examine the expectations underlying our guilt, we can begin asking healthier questions:

  • Is this expectation realistic?
  • Would I hold a loved one or friend to this standard?
  • Am I responsible for this outcome?
  • What do my values, rather than my expectations, tell me to do?

As Reid's work reminds us, a meaningful life is not built on endless self-sacrifice. It is built on alignment with our values, self-respect, and the courage to let go of expectations that were never ours to carry.

In summary, the goal is not to eliminate guilt entirely. The goal is to make room for the kind of guilt that guides us, while releasing the guilt that merely weighs us down.

For those interested in learning more about guilt, Dr. Jennifer Reid's interview on Wellness in Today's World provides a deeper understanding of adaptive and excessive guilt, the sources of it, and how to access more joy, agency, and freedom in your life.
